step1_summary.chief_complaint: Very itchy, sore red skin for 4 days, seeking quick treatment.

symptoms.location: Chest, hands, arms (including inside the elbows/antecubital fossae); not on face
symptoms.character: Intense pruritus (worse at night, prevents sleep), sore, dry, some cracked skin/fissuring
symptoms.severity: Severe — interferes with sleep, concentration at work
symptoms.aggravating_factors: Not clearly identified; patient notes symptoms worse with activity (hiking) previously made eczema painful, uses showers to try to ease itching
symptoms.alleviating_factors: Tried OTC steroid cream last night (no benefit yet), tried antihistamines (patient says they did not help)

step1_summary.past_medical_history: Prior eczema (localized to arms previously). Past asthma (not active). No other chronic conditions reported.

medications_allergies.recent_medications/OTC: OTC topical steroid cream purchased last night; has tried antihistamines recently (type unspecified)

family_social_history.occupation: Project manager at a pharmaceutical company (works full time)
family_social_history.alcohol: Occasional — a few beers per week

step1_summary.vitals_exam_findings: No documented vitals. Doctor noted dry, cracked skin and a rash that appeared 'familiar' on viewing; no bleeding, no pus/discharge. No systemic features reported (no fever, cough, breathing difficulty).

V: Acute urticaria / urticarial reaction: Vascular-mediated wheals can cause intensely itchy, red lesions on trunk and limbs; could present acutely over days.

Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (less likely): Can cause red/painful/palpable purpura and systemic symptoms, sometimes pruritic — considered because of new widespread rash, but presentation in transcript lacks typical features.
I: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare: Prior history of eczema, distribution includes antecubital fossae and arms, dry/cracked skin and intense itch are classic for eczema flare.
Scabies infestation: Intense nocturnal itch and involvement of hands/wrists/axilla/torso with household contacts possible — scabies can present acutely when exposure occurs.

Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization/Staph aureus): Cracked/ fissured eczematous skin can become secondarily infected, which can increase soreness — considered given cracked skin, though no pus or systemic signs reported.
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (e.g., mycosis fungoides) (less likely): Chronic, pruritic, patchy rash can mimic eczema but typically has more chronic course than 4 days.
Skin malignancy/metastatic lesions (very unlikely): Focal lesions would be expected; acute generalized itch without other signs argues against.
D: Xerosis (environmental dry skin) with eczematization: Dry skin can lead to cracking and pruritus and precipitate eczema-like flares — plausible as an exacerbating factor.
Nutritional deficiency–related pruritus (e.g., iron, niacin) (less likely): Typically more chronic/systemic features; acute onset less consistent.
I2: Irritant or allergic contact dermatitis to a new topical product or clothing (including OTC cream excipients): New or irritating products can cause acute itchy, red, cracked skin; patient unsure about triggers.
Topical steroid reaction or misuse (less likely here): Withdrawal reactions occur with chronic potent steroid use; patient only used OTC steroid last night, so unlikely to explain the initial onset.
C: Inherited ichthyosis/keratinization disorders (unlikely): These cause chronic dry, scaly skin from early life rather than acute 4-day onset.
A: Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity): Can present acutely with intensely itchy erythematous rash in exposed areas — relevant if patient had exposure to a new soap, detergent, or topical agent.
Atopic dermatitis (immune-mediated component): Overlaps with inflammatory category but is immune-driven and linked to history of eczema.
T: Irritant dermatitis from friction/chafing (e.g., from hiking gear/clothing): Patient mentions hiking and that activity previously made skin 'painful' — friction or sweat may trigger/exacerbate rash.
E: Cholestatic pruritus or systemic pruritus from endocrine/metabolic disease (e.g., liver disease, thyroid disease): Can cause intense generalized itch; however, absence of systemic symptoms and acute onset make these less likely.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient has prior history of eczema, current distribution includes antecubital fossae/arms and chest, findings of dry, cracked skin and intense pruritus interfering with sleep are classic for an eczema flare; doctor also clinically suspected this and recommended topical steroid + emollients.
supporting_evidence: Distribution: arms/inside elbows (antecubital fossae) and chest — common sites for atopic dermatitis
Dry, cracked skin with intense itching and soreness
Physician noted rash appeared 'familiar' and recommended stronger topical steroid and emollients
opposing_evidence: Current flare is more widespread than prior eczema (prior was mainly on arms), though atopic flares can change distribution
No prior sustained response to OTC steroid last night (but too soon to judge effectiveness)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis (or irritant contact dermatitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute, intensely itchy, erythematous, cracked skin can be caused by contact dermatitis to a new soap, detergent, clothing, or topical agent; patient lives with flatmates (possible shared products) and is unsure about triggers. Contact dermatitis can present suddenly and extensively depending on exposure.
supporting_evidence: Acute onset over days with prominent itch
Widespread involvement including chest and hands (areas that may contact allergens/irritants)
Patient uncertain about triggers and advised to keep a diary of potential triggers (doctor suggestion)
opposing_evidence: Patient reports no known recent changes in shower gel/clothing or known exposures
No clear contact distribution (e.g., localized to exposed sites) described

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Scabies causes intense nocturnal pruritus, commonly affects hands/wrists/axillae/trunk, and household contacts can be involved. Acute intense itch with involvement of hands and trunk raises possibility, particularly given living with flatmates.
supporting_evidence: Severe itching, worse at night (patient reports inability to sleep)
opposing_evidence: Patient did not report classic burrows, interdigital web involvement, or involvement of genitalia; doctor did not document typical scabies signs
Onset was over several days; scabies can present within this timeframe but often evolves with classic distribution which was not explicitly described

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Xerosis with eczematization (dry skin causing/triggering flare)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dry skin can precipitate severe itch and cracking and can precipitate or worsen eczematous inflammation. The patient reports dry, cracked skin and uses showers to try to ease itch, suggesting dryness may be contributory.
supporting_evidence: Patient finds showering briefly eases itching (common with xerosis)
Physician recommended emollients as part of treatment
opposing_evidence: Abrupt 4-day onset of severe symptoms is more suggestive of an inflammatory trigger or infestation than simple chronic xerosis alone

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Secondary bacterial infection of eczematous skin
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Cracked eczematous skin can become colonized or infected, increasing soreness. However, there is no reported pus, bleeding, systemic signs, or focal cellulitis to support active infection at this time.
supporting_evidence: Cracked/sore skin which can predispose to bacterial entry
opposing_evidence: No pus, drainage, malodour, fever, or localised warmth/erythema documented
